items.note: SHAPES: C k x n maps state to measurement, Q k x k. ROBOT: GPS on the drone: C = [I_3 0], k = 3; a single range sensor: k = 1.

The measurement likelihood p(z|x). Its log is the quadratic in 3.35 that the update minimises. ROBOT: this is also your outlier test: a measurement with tiny p(z|x) under the predicted belief is a candidate outlier (gate, card C5).
Gaussian prior. ROBOT: on the real robot you rarely have one; a huge Sigma_0 is the usual hack and it is exactly what the information filter (3.5) handles cleanly with Omega = 0.

items.anchor: The mean is updated using the deterministic version of the state transition function
items.note: WHY: predict mean = run the model with zero noise. In the EKF this becomes g(u, mu) with the FULL nonlinear g (card C2, bug class 1).

items.anchor: This matrix is multiplied twice into the covariance, since the covariance is a quadratic matrix
items.note: WHY: Cov(A x) = A Cov(x) A^T. Any linear map pushes a covariance through 'once per side'. Same reason Jacobians appear as G Sigma G^T in 3.3 and as the sandwich in Joseph form.

items.anchor: It specifies the degree to which the measurement is incorporated into the new state estimate
items.note: DEFINE: Kalman gain. Intuition: K -> 0 when the sensor is bad (Q large) or the prior is confident (Sigma_bar small); K -> C^+ when the sensor is perfect. SESSION: Fig 2.2a slider sigma_z^2 shows exactly this.

items.anchor: adjusting for the information gain resulting from the measurement
items.note: WHY: line 6 is where the covariance shrinks. It never depends on z itself: in a linear KF the covariance sequence can be computed offline before any data arrives (this is what makes steady-state / precomputed-gain KFs possible on microcontrollers).

items.anchor: the measurement space is much lower dimensional than the state space
items.note: ROBOT: EKF-SLAM: n = 3 + 2N landmarks, k = 2 per observation. The O(n^2) term in line 6 is the cost you pay per landmark observation; ch. 10 shows how to keep it from being O(n^3).

items.note: WHY: the posterior mean is a precision-weighted average of prior and measurement. With equal precisions it is the midpoint; the gain K is the weight.

items.anchor: measurement update step
items.note: DEFINE: measurement update (lines 4-6) vs prediction step (lines 2-3). Thrun's names; Bar-Shalom says 'correction' and 'time update'.

items.anchor: When multiplying two Gaussians, for example, the exponents add
items.note: THE IDEA of the whole derivation: product of Gaussians = sum of quadratics = another quadratic = another Gaussian. Everything else is bookkeeping. Same fact makes factor graphs work: a sum of quadratic factors is one big quadratic.

Bayes prediction (2.41) with both factors Gaussian. The integral over x_{t-1} is marginalisation; for Gaussians, marginalising = dropping rows/columns of Sigma, which is why the result is closed-form.
L_t: the exponent, quadratic in both x_{t-1} and x_t. Keep this picture: L_t is a paraboloid; 'integrate out x_{t-1}' = slide along one axis and keep the minimum.

The split L_t = L_t(x_{t-1}, x_t) + L_t(x_t). Completing the square. In factor-graph language this is marginalising x_{t-1} via the Schur complement; GTSAM does this every time it eliminates a variable.
Psi_t^{-1} = A^T R^{-1} A + Sigma_{t-1}^{-1}: the curvature (information) of L_t in x_{t-1}. Its inverse is the conditional covariance of x_{t-1} given x_t. This is the Schur complement in disguise.
Solving the first-order condition for x_{t-1}. Five lines of pure algebra; do it once by hand (T2 extension) and never again.

items.anchor: The important thing to notice is that the value of this integral is independent
items.note: WHY the trick works: the x_{t-1}-part integrates to a constant that does not depend on x_t, so it vanishes into eta. This is the one sentence to understand in 3.2.4.

L_t(x_t) with all x_{t-1} terms cancelled. From here: first derivative -> mean (3.31), second derivative -> inverse covariance (3.32). Pattern to remember: mean = argmin of the quadratic, covariance = inverse Hessian. Same in every least-squares estimator (Gauss-Newton gives the covariance for free).
First use of the inversion lemma: (R + A Sigma A^T)^{-1} appears, which is the predicted information. Watch for the pattern 'something^{-1} + P^T Q^{-1} P' - it always means the lemma applies.

items.anchor: The (specialized) inversion lemma, sometimes called the
items.note: Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury. Memorise the shape: (R + P Q P^T)^{-1} = R^{-1} - R^{-1} P (Q^{-1} + P^T R^{-1} P)^{-1} P^T R^{-1}. It trades an n x n inversion for a k x k one. T2.1 uses it; card C5 explains why GTSAM's Marginals is expensive.
Second derivative of L_t(x_t) = (A Sigma A^T + R)^{-1}. Inverse Hessian = covariance. This proves line 3 of Table 3.1.
Bayes measurement update (2.38) with both factors Gaussian: posterior ∝ likelihood x prior. No integral this time, so the update derivation is shorter than the prediction one.

J_t: sum of two quadratics, measurement residual weighted by Q^{-1} plus prior residual weighted by Sigma_bar^{-1}. This is exactly a weighted least-squares cost. MHE (t7.4) minimises the same thing over a window; the KF solves it for one step.
Hessian of J_t = C^T Q^{-1} C + Sigma_bar^{-1}: posterior information = measurement information + prior information. Information ADDS. This single line is the entire information filter (3.5).
Line 5 proved. Note the form: posterior mean = prior mean + gain x innovation. Every recursive estimator you will meet (RLS, complementary filter, PX4 EKF2) has this shape.

K rewritten so it uses Sigma_bar instead of Sigma_t (breaks the circularity with line 6). Eight lines of algebra with 'insert I' tricks; skim, but notice the destination: the inversion is now of the k x k matrix C Sigma_bar C^T + Q.
Inversion lemma applied to the posterior information. This turns 'add information, then invert n x n' into 'subtract a k-rank correction'. Line 6 of the KF is the second form.
Line 6 proved: Sigma = (I - K C) Sigma_bar. CODE: in floating point this form loses symmetry; the Joseph form (card C1, T2.2) is the same quantity written as a sandwich. T4 bug 4.

items.note: WHY the EKF exists: no closed form, so approximate. Two approximations are possible: approximate the FUNCTION (EKF: tangent) or approximate the DISTRIBUTION (UKF: sigma points; PF: samples). Keep this taxonomy.

items.anchor: The goal of the EKF is thus shifted from computing the exact posterior
items.note: DEFINE: the EKF's belief is an approximation of an approximation: a Gaussian fitted to a non-Gaussian truth, with parameters estimated via linearisation. Two error sources; 3.3.5 names the second.

items.anchor: Projecting the Gaussian through this linear approximation results in a Gaussian density

Linearised motion density. The mean uses g(u, mu_{t-1}) exactly; only the SPREAD uses G. Keep the two apart in code (card C2).
Linearised measurement density around mu_bar_t. H evaluated at the predicted mean: you must predict before you linearise the measurement.

items.note: FIGURE 3.6: same prior width, different mean. The mean in (a) sits where g bends; (b) where g is nearly straight. The EKF cannot tell the difference; it only sees the slope at the mean.

items.anchor: moments matching
items.note: DEFINE: moments matching / assumed density filter: choose the Gaussian whose mean and covariance equal the TRUE output moments. Optimal among Gaussians; usually needs Monte Carlo or analytic integrals. The UKF is a cheap deterministic approximation of this.

items.anchor: which performs a stochastic linearization through the use of a weighted statistical linear regression
items.note: DEFINE: statistical linearisation: fit a line through g by weighted regression over sigma points instead of taking the derivative at one point. That is why the UKF is derivative-free and why it sees curvature.

items.anchor: these sigma points are located at the mean and symmetrically along the main axes of the covariance
items.note: GEOMETRY: 2n+1 points: centre, plus/minus one scaled step along each column of a square root of Sigma. With a symmetric square root the steps lie on the ellipse's principal axes; with Cholesky they lie on a different but equally valid set of directions (card C3 trick 1). SESSION Fig 2.2b.

items.note: beta encodes prior knowledge of the distribution's kurtosis. beta = 2 for Gaussian priors. alpha and kappa control spread; values are convention, not theory (card C3 trick 4 shows what small alpha does to the weights).
Push each sigma point through g. 2n+1 evaluations of the real nonlinear function; no derivative anywhere. CODE: card C3 line 3.

items.note: RESULT: UT exact to second order in the Taylor expansion of the mean (for Gaussian priors, to third order in odd terms by symmetry); EKF exact to first. SESSION Fig 2.2b tile '2nd-order term' shows the size of what the EKF misses: -r sigma_theta^2 / 2.

items.note: TEST: for linear g, h the UKF equals the KF exactly. exercises/tests::test_unscented_transform_is_exact_for_linear_maps checks this; it is the first thing to verify in any UKF implementation.

items.anchor: In many practical applications, the difference between EKF and UKF is negligible
items.note: PRACTICAL: when Sigma is small and dt is short, EKF = UKF. Choose by engineering: UKF when Jacobians are painful or g is a black box; EKF when you need the Jacobian anyway (e.g. for smoothing / factor graphs later).

items.anchor: the sigma points of the unscented transform are determined deterministically, while particle filters draw samples randomly
items.note: UKF vs PF in one sentence. 2n+1 deterministic points vs thousands of random ones. UKF wins when the truth is roughly Gaussian; PF wins when it is not. ch. 4 next.

items.anchor: what is computationally complex in one parameterization happens to be simple in the other
items.note: THE DUALITY. Table in lecture L5. Decide which filter by which operation dominates: many measurements per motion step -> IF; many motion steps per measurement -> KF.
xi = Sigma^{-1} mu, the information vector. Not a state: it is the mean scaled by precision. Recovering mu needs a solve (3.73). CODE: card C5, never inv(Omega) @ xi.

Expanding the Gaussian exponent: -1/2 x^T Sigma^{-1} x + x^T Sigma^{-1} mu + const. The quadratic term carries Omega, the linear term carries xi. This is why information form is natural for products: exponents add term by term.
-log p(x) = const + 1/2 x^T Omega x - x^T xi: a quadratic. Every least-squares SLAM back-end minimises a sum of these. The negative log of a Gaussian IS a least-squares cost.
Setting the gradient to zero: Omega x = xi. The posterior mean is the solution of a linear system; solve it with Cholesky (or sparse Cholesky, which is what GTSAM/iSAM do). Never form Omega^{-1}.

items.anchor: The output are the parameters ξt and Ωt of the updated Gaussian
items.note: Table 3.5 I/O is canonical in, canonical out; no mean is ever formed. That is only possible because the models are linear. The EIF (3.5.4) loses this.
Same models as 3.2 and 3.5. The information filter is not a different model, only a different coordinate system for the belief.

items.anchor: involves the inversion of two matrices of the size
items.note: COST: two n x n inversions per predict. ROBOT: a 1000-landmark map in information form would invert 2003 x 2003 twice per motion step. Ch. 12 (SEIF) avoids this by exploiting sparsity; this sentence is the motivation for that whole chapter.

items.anchor: Measurement updates are additive in the information filter
items.note: COST: update = add two matrices. ROBOT: fusing 64 beams of a LiDAR scan in one step is 64 additions in information form and 64 k x k inversions in covariance form.
IF prediction derived by substituting Sigma = Omega^{-1} into 3.83 and inverting back. Nothing deep; the expense is in the two inversions this substitution creates.

The update in exponent form: posterior Omega and xi are literally read off the brackets. Compare with the KF update derivation (3.35-3.47): twelve equations there, three here. That is the duality in action.
Omega_t = C^T Q^{-1} C + Omega_bar_t. Information adds. CODE: card C5 if_update. TEST: test_information_form_round_trip_and_update_equals_kf and test_information_form_accepts_total_ignorance.

items.anchor: This mandates the recovery of a state estimate μ from the canonical parameters
items.note: PITFALL of the EIF: g and h need a point to be evaluated/linearised at, so mu = Omega^{-1} xi must be recovered every step (Table 3.6 lines 2 and 5). The clean canonical-in/canonical-out property of Table 3.5 is lost.

items.anchor: Table 3.6
items.note: EIF = EKF in information coordinates. Lines 2 and 5 recover means (two solves); 3 is the expensive prediction; 6-7 are additive updates with the linearised measurement. IMPLEMENT only if you go on to ch. 12; otherwise read for the structure.
G and H defined exactly as in the EKF (3.51, 3.53). One Jacobian code path serves both filters.
EIF measurement update. Notice the extra term H_t mu_bar_t inside the bracket of 3.107: it is the linearisation constant h(mu_bar) - H mu_bar moved to the information vector. Easy to drop by mistake.

items.anchor: The information filter tends to be numerically more stable
items.note: PRACTICAL: Omega is built by adding PSD terms, so it stays PSD; Sigma in the KF is built by subtracting (line 6), which is where round-off makes it indefinite. Another reason square-root and information-form filters exist.

items.anchor: the integration á la Kalman filter induces severe computational problems
items.note: ROBOT: a dense Sigma couples every variable to every other; one new measurement touches all n^2 entries. Information form lets you add locally. This is the seed of SEIF (ch. 12) and of every sparse SLAM solver.

items.anchor: Addition is commutative
items.note: WHY multi-robot fusion is easy in information form: each robot contributes C^T Q^{-1} C and C^T Q^{-1} z; sum them in any order, at any time. Delayed or out-of-order measurements need no reprocessing. ROBOT: iRAP multi-robot mapping.

items.anchor: the information filter is generally believed to be computationally inferior to the Kalman filter
items.note: The honest verdict for DENSE problems: EIF loses because of the state recovery and the prediction inversions. The IF wins only when Omega is sparse, which is the next paragraph and the rest of the SLAM literature.

items.anchor: the interaction of state variables is local
items.note: WHY Omega is sparse in SLAM: a landmark only interacts with the poses that observed it. Zero in Omega = conditional independence. Zero in Sigma would mean marginal independence, which never holds (everything is coupled through the robot path).

items.anchor: loopy belief propagation
items.note: DEFINE: inference on a sparse Gaussian graph by passing messages. Related to Gauss-Seidel and to iSAM's incremental updates. Not needed now; recognise the name when it appears in ch. 12.

items.anchor: The result of this operation is a matrix known as the Jacobian
items.note: SUMMARY check: can you write G for the velocity model from memory? If not, exercise T3.2 before moving on.

items.anchor: The primary disadvantage is their confinement to unimodal Gaussian distributions
items.note: The one limitation none of the four filters removes. Ch. 4 (histogram and particle filters) is the answer; the price is exponential cost in n.

items.anchor: the Kalman filter and its nonlinear extension, the extended Kalman filter, are vastly more popular
items.note: Why you will see EKFs everywhere in robotics code (PX4, ArduPilot, robot_localization) and information filters mostly inside SLAM back-ends.

items.anchor: The unscented Kalman filter is due to Julier and Uhlmann (1997)
items.note: READING: Julier & Uhlmann 1997 for the UT; van der Merwe 2004 (thesis) for the sigma-point family and the square-root UKF you would use in production.

items.anchor: What is a minimal state vector for the Kalman filter
items.note: EXERCISE 1(a) answer shape: (p, v) suffices because acceleration is white noise; adding acceleration would make the noise non-Markov in the smaller state. exercises/models.py::CarCV encodes 1(b)-(c); test_book_exercise_1c_five_steps_from_rest checks (c).

items.anchor: you can create those ellipses by analyzing the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix
items.note: HOW: eigen-decompose Sigma; semi-axes = sqrt(eigenvalues) x n_sigma along the eigenvectors. CODE: viz.py style.cov_ellipse does this; SESSION Fig 2.2a draws 1-sigma and 2-sigma.
